blocks.content: An operating system is the software that sits between you and the hardware of a computer. Every time you open an app, save a file, or connect to the internet, the operating system is quietly making it happen. It is the most important piece of software on any device, because nothing else can run without it.

This chapter explains what an operating system really is, why computers need one, how it works underneath, the components and services it offers, the different kinds you will meet, and how to talk about it in an interview.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408307681-380919767.png
1. Introduction and Why We Need One
blocks.text: 1. Introduction and Why We Need One

blocks.content: A computer is made of hardware such as the processor, memory, storage, and input and output devices. On its own, this hardware is just electronics that cannot do anything useful. It needs one special piece of software to coordinate everything, and that software is the operating system, often shortened to OS. When you press the power button, it is the first major program to load, and once running it takes control of the hardware and offers a friendly environment where your applications can run.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: An operating system is the software that manages a computer hardware and resources and provides services that applications and users rely on.
Why we need an operating system
blocks.text: Why we need an operating system

blocks.content: Imagine there was no operating system. Every single application would have to talk directly to the hardware, and each one would need to know exactly how your particular keyboard, disk, and graphics card work. Without a coordinator, several problems appear immediately.

["Two programs could try to use the same memory at once and corrupt each other.","Every developer would have to write code for every possible piece of hardware.","There would be no fair way to share the processor, so one program could freeze the machine.","There would be no protection, so a buggy or malicious program could destroy everything."]
items: Two programs could try to use the same memory at once and corrupt each other.
Every developer would have to write code for every possible piece of hardware.
There would be no fair way to share the processor, so one program could freeze the machine.
There would be no protection, so a buggy or malicious program could destroy everything.

blocks.content: /engineering/library/os/images/1785408307683-950628110.png
blocks.alt: Why we need an operating system

blocks.content: The operating system solves all of this by acting as a central manager. Applications ask for what they need, and the operating system decides how to give it to them safely and fairly.
Life without an operating system

Some very small devices, such as a simple digital thermometer, run a single fixed program directly on the hardware with no operating system at all. For anything more capable, though, its absence would be crippling. You could run only one program at a time, there would be no files or folders, and no protection if that program had a bug. The operating system is what turns raw hardware into a flexible, multi purpose machine.

blocks.title: A way to picture it
blocks.content: Hardware without an operating system is like an orchestra with no conductor. Every instrument is capable, but there is no one to bring them together into music.
2. What an Operating System Is
There are a few ways to define an operating system, and each highlights a different angle. Together they give a complete picture.

["As a resource manager: it controls and allocates the processor, memory, storage, and devices among all the programs that want them.","As an interface: it provides a bridge between the user and the hardware, so people and programs do not deal with raw electronics.","As a control program: it manages the execution of programs and prevents errors and misuse of the computer."]
items: As a resource manager: it controls and allocates the processor, memory, storage, and devices among all the programs that want them.
As an interface: it provides a bridge between the user and the hardware, so people and programs do not deal with raw electronics.
As a control program: it manages the execution of programs and prevents errors and misuse of the computer.

blocks.content: An operating system is a program that acts as an intermediary between a user of a computer and the computer hardware, managing resources and providing a platform for applications to run.

blocks.title: A real-world analogy
blocks.content: Think of a busy hotel. Guests want rooms, food, and cleaning, but they never go into the kitchen or boiler room themselves. The management coordinates everything behind the scenes and gives each guest a smooth experience. The operating system is that management, the applications are the guests, the hardware is the rooms and staff, and the front desk is the interface you interact with.
3. Responsibilities of an Operating System
The operating system carries several major responsibilities at the same time. Each is a whole field of study, but at a high level they are easy to understand.

["Process management: deciding which program runs on the processor and when, and switching between them quickly.","Memory management: tracking which parts of memory are used, giving memory to programs, and reclaiming it when they finish.","File and storage management: organizing data into files and folders and controlling how they are read and written.","Device management: talking to hardware such as the keyboard, printer, and disk through drivers.","Security and protection: keeping programs and users from interfering with each other or the system."]
items: Process management: deciding which program runs on the processor and when, and switching between them quickly.
Memory management: tracking which parts of memory are used, giving memory to programs, and reclaiming it when they finish.
File and storage management: organizing data into files and folders and controlling how they are read and written.
Device management: talking to hardware such as the keyboard, printer, and disk through drivers.
Security and protection: keeping programs and users from interfering with each other or the system.

blocks.content: /engineering/library/os/images/1785408307683-32843304.png
Why it is called a resource manager
blocks.text: Why it is called a resource manager

blocks.content: The processor, memory, storage, and devices are all limited resources, and many programs want them at the same time. Something must decide who gets what and when, which is exactly the job of a manager. The operating system decides which process runs on the processor, hands out memory and takes it back, controls access to files and devices, and tracks usage so no single program can starve the others. It treats the hardware as a set of scarce resources and shares them efficiently and fairly.
4. How It Works and Acts as an Interface
blocks.text: 4. How It Works and Acts as an Interface

blocks.content: When the computer starts, a small program stored in firmware runs first, checks the hardware, and loads the core of the operating system, called the kernel, into memory. From that moment the kernel is in charge. It runs in a protected mode with full access to the hardware, while your applications run in a limited mode called user mode. When an application needs something only the kernel can do, such as reading a file, it makes a request called a system call. The kernel checks the request, performs the operation safely, and returns the result.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408307683-931500445.png
blocks.alt: How It Works and Acts as an Interface

blocks.title: User mode and kernel mode
blocks.content: This split is the heart of how an operating system stays safe. Ordinary programs cannot touch hardware directly; they must go through the kernel, which can say no to unsafe requests.
The operating system as an interface
blocks.text: The operating system as an interface

blocks.content: Hardware speaks in electrical signals and machine instructions that no person or program wants to deal with. The operating system sits in the middle and translates between the two worlds. For users, the interface is the shell, which can be a graphical desktop or a command line. For programs, the interface is the set of system calls the operating system exposes. Whether you are a person clicking an icon or a program requesting a file, you never touch the hardware directly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408307684-472298219.png
blocks.alt: The operating system as an interface

blocks.title: Two kinds of interface
blocks.content: The operating system offers a user interface for people, through a desktop or command line, and a programming interface for applications, through system calls. Both shield you from the raw hardware.
5. Major Components of an Operating System
blocks.text: 5. Major Components of an Operating System

blocks.content: An operating system is not a single block. It is built from several cooperating parts.

{"headers":["Component","What it does"],"rows":[["Kernel","The core that manages the processor, memory, and devices and runs in privileged mode"],["Process scheduler","Decides which process runs next and for how long"],["Memory manager","Allocates and frees memory and enables virtual memory"],["File system","Organizes data into files and directories on storage"],["Device drivers","Translate general requests into commands a specific device understands"],["Shell","The interface, either command line or graphical, that lets users give commands"]]}
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408307684-705254094.png
blocks.alt: Major Components of an Operating System

blocks.content: The kernel is the most important component. A helpful mental model is to picture it at the center, with the scheduler, memory manager, file system, and drivers as arms reaching out to control each resource, and the shell wrapped around the outside as the face the user sees.
6. Services Provided by an Operating System
blocks.text: 6. Services Provided by an Operating System

blocks.content: From the point of view of a program, the operating system is a provider of useful services. Instead of doing hard, dangerous work itself, a program simply asks for a service.

["Program execution: loading a program into memory and running it, then cleaning up when it ends.","Input and output operations: handling reads and writes to devices so programs do not have to.","File system access: creating, opening, reading, writing, and deleting files.","Communication: letting processes exchange data with each other and across networks.","Error detection: noticing hardware faults and program errors and responding safely.","Resource allocation: sharing the processor, memory, and devices among many programs."]
items: Program execution: loading a program into memory and running it, then cleaning up when it ends.
Input and output operations: handling reads and writes to devices so programs do not have to.
File system access: creating, opening, reading, writing, and deleting files.
Communication: letting processes exchange data with each other and across networks.
Error detection: noticing hardware faults and program errors and responding safely.
Resource allocation: sharing the processor, memory, and devices among many programs.

blocks.content: 7. Types of Operating Systems
Operating systems come in several types, each shaped by the kind of work it was built for.

{"headers":["Type","Idea","Where it is used"],"rows":[["Batch","Jobs are collected and run in groups with little interaction","Old mainframe payroll and billing"],["Time sharing","Many users share one machine, each getting quick turns","Multi user servers"],["Distributed","Many computers work together and appear as one system","Large scale computing clusters"],["Real time","Responses must happen within strict time limits","Medical devices, car controls, robotics"],["Embedded","A small operating system built into a device for one job","Routers, smart appliances"],["Mobile","Designed for phones with touch, battery, and app stores","Android, iOS"]]}

blocks.title: General purpose systems blend types
blocks.content: The operating system on your laptop is mostly a time sharing, multitasking system, but it also borrows real time ideas for tasks such as audio so sound never stutters.
8. Examples of Operating Systems
You already use operating systems every day, even if you never think about them by name.

{"headers":["Operating system","Common on","Note"],"rows":[["Windows","Desktops and laptops","The most widely used desktop OS"],["Linux","Servers and developers machines","Open source and highly customizable"],["macOS","Apple computers","Built on a Unix foundation"],["Android","Phones and tablets","Based on the Linux kernel"],["iOS","iPhones","Apple mobile operating system"]]}

blocks.title: A useful fact
blocks.content: Android and much of the internet run on the Linux kernel. Learning basic Linux concepts pays off far beyond a single device.
9. Advantages and Limitations
The operating system exists because the benefits are enormous. Without it, modern computing would be impossible.

["It lets many programs run at the same time by sharing the processor.","It hides hardware complexity so developers write to the operating system, not to each device.","It protects programs and users from each other, improving stability and security.","It manages memory efficiently and gives each program the illusion of its own space.","It provides a consistent, friendly interface for users through a shell or desktop."]
items: It lets many programs run at the same time by sharing the processor.
It hides hardware complexity so developers write to the operating system, not to each device.
It protects programs and users from each other, improving stability and security.
It manages memory efficiently and gives each program the illusion of its own space.
It provides a consistent, friendly interface for users through a shell or desktop.

blocks.content: It is not free of cost, though, and it is worth being honest about the tradeoffs.

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Enables multitasking and safe sharing of hardware","It consumes memory and processing power for itself"],["Hides complexity from application developers","A bug or crash in the kernel can bring down the whole machine"],["Adds strong protection and security boundaries","It is complex software that can contain security vulnerabilities"],["","Layers of management add a small overhead to every operation"]]}
These limitations are the price of coordination. The overhead of the operating system is tiny compared to the chaos of having no coordinator at all.
10. What Happens When You Open an Application
blocks.text: 10. What Happens When You Open an Application

blocks.content: Let us make everything concrete by tracing what happens when you double click an application, such as a music player.

["You click the icon, and the shell tells the operating system to launch that program.","The operating system finds the program file on storage through the file system.","The memory manager allocates memory and loads the program into it, creating a process.","The scheduler gives that process time on the processor so it can start running.","When the app plays a song, it makes system calls to read the file and send sound to the speaker.","When you close the app, the operating system frees its memory and cleans up the process."]
items: You click the icon, and the shell tells the operating system to launch that program.
The operating system finds the program file on storage through the file system.
The memory manager allocates memory and loads the program into it, creating a process.
The scheduler gives that process time on the processor so it can start running.
When the app plays a song, it makes system calls to read the file and send sound to the speaker.
When you close the app, the operating system frees its memory and cleans up the process.

blocks.content: /engineering/library/os/images/1785408307684-851823102.png
blocks.alt: What Happens When You Open an Application

blocks.content: Every step relies on the operating system. The application never touches the disk, memory, or speaker directly; it simply asks, and the operating system does the work safely.
